syllabus.clause: why plain LRU is flushed by one large scan

at.step: Can a cache remember something besides recency?

syllabus.clause: ghost lists and adaptive partitioning in ARC (Megiddo & Modha, FAST 2003)

sources.source: Johnson and Shasha, "2Q: A Low Overhead High Performance Buffer Management Replacement Algorithm"

items.item: The three-queue structure (Am, A1in capped at Kin, A1out capped at Kout) and the recommended sizing of twenty-five and fifty percent
A ghost entry costs only an identifier, a few bytes, never the page's data

at.step: What does a ghost entry cost?

items.item: 2Q's own measured scan-resistance result (retains about seventy percent of its no-scan hit rate, vs. about sixty percent for LRU)

sources.source: Megiddo and Modha, "ARC: A Self-Tuning, Low Overhead Replacement Cache"

items.item: ARC needs no offline-selected tuning parameters and keeps no frequency counts
ARC's directory remembers twice as many pages as fit in the cache
Redis's LFU counter: a probabilistic, logarithmic eight-bit counter, with tunable log factor and decay time, defaults of ten and one minute
PostgreSQL replaced ARC with 2Q in 8.0.2 to avoid a pending US patent on ARC, then moved to clock sweep in 8.1

sources.source: Wikipedia: "LIRS caching algorithm" (secondary source; primary paper unreachable)

items.item: Reuse distance (distinct pages touched since a page's own last use) as LIRS's locality metric, and the resident LIR/HIR partition
LIRS's real deployment, including MySQL since version 5.1

sources.source: Zhang et al., "SIEVE is Simpler than LRU" (NSDI 2024)

items.item: SIEVE's own abstract: under twenty lines of code change on average across five production cache libraries, up to sixty-three point two percent lower miss ratio than ARC on 1559 traces

expert.by: self-review (no independent reviewer this session; see REVIEW.md)

items.item: Why a pure frequency count is the wrong fix on its own: it survives a scan but never forgets, so a page that was hot once stays privileged forever even after it stops being touched
Why a ghost list is the cheapest possible form of 'memory' a cache can keep: an identifier costs a few bytes, versus the full page a resident entry would cost

at.step: What does a ghost entry cost?

items.item: Why a scan's pages pass through 2Q's first-time queue into the ghost list without ever reaching the protected LRU list: a single touch is never enough to earn promotion, only a second touch while still remembered as a ghost is

That a ghost hit is itself the signal ARC adapts on: a hit in B1 means the recency list was too small, a hit in B2 means the frequency list was too small, and the adjustment is proportional to the two ghost lists' relative sizes

at.step: What does a ghost hit say?

items.item: Why ARC, with zero reuse ever, degrades to exactly plain LRU with no ghost-list overhead at all — ghosts only start forming once at least one key has been promoted out of the recency list, which is what the hand trace in examples.py had to arrange for

The distinction between recency (how long ago, counting every intervening access) and reuse distance (how many distinct keys, ignoring repeats) — LIRS's whole mechanism rests on using the second instead of the first

Why LIRS survives a loop slightly larger than the cache where LRU gets zero hits: the loop's own reuse distance is finite and bounded by the loop's length, so a low-reuse-distance set sized to the loop stays resident across every pass

That each of the four policies costs something extra per entry or per access for the thing it remembers beyond recency: a counter and a decay tick for LFU, a ghost identifier for 2Q and ARC, a distinction between two resident sets for LIRS — none of this is free

at.deep: Production failures this topic warns about

items.item: The explicit caveat that LIRS's claims here trace to a secondary description, not the original paper, because the paper is unreachable from this research session — a fact a careless reader could otherwise miss

That PostgreSQL's own production history (shipped ARC, replaced it for a patent concern, then moved to a third, different policy) shows that even a theoretically strong policy can lose to a licensing constraint in practice, independent of its measured performance
